title: Minorities from three neighbours who came without papers must now get visas to stay
dek: A Home Ministry order keeps the shield against prosecution for six non-Muslim communities from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who arrived by 2024, but makes continued stay depend on a visa. It also tightens ID rules on the Nepal and Bhutan borders.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
People from six non-Muslim communities who came to India from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan without valid papers will now have to obtain an "appropriate" Indian visa if they want to keep living here, under an amendment the Union Home Ministry notified this week. The change affects many people in West Bengal who crossed from Bangladesh.

The Immigration and Foreigners (Exemption) (Amendment) Order, 2026 keeps the existing rule that Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis and Christians from the three countries who entered India on or before 31 December 2024, fleeing religious persecution or the fear of it, cannot be penalised for arriving without a passport or visa. But it adds a condition, quoted by The Hindu: "every such person shall be required to obtain an appropriate category of visa after their entry into India for their continued stay in India."

## What the order says

The Hindu reported that the amendment was notified on Wednesday, 4 November; PTI, in a report carried by DT Next, said it was published in the gazette on Thursday. It is issued under the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, which replaced the old passport and foreigners laws last year.

The exemption covers people who entered without valid passports or travel documents, and those whose documents have since expired. According to The Hindu, the new visa condition replaces a rule that required such people to register with the authorities within 14 days after completing 180 days in India.

The same visa condition is applied to three smaller groups of long-term residents who cannot renew their foreign passports, PTI reported:

- Pakistani nationals who entered India on or before 31 December 2009 intending to settle permanently and cannot renew their passports because they do not hold a Pakistani national identity card. They must not have married or bought property in Pakistan, must have Indian-citizen family members, must undertake not to return to Pakistan, and must have no adverse police or security reports.
- People of Indian origin who took Malaysian or Singaporean citizenship and returned to India on or before 31 December 2009, whose passports have expired.
- Certain Partition-era migrants who returned from Pakistan and settled in Kerala, according to The Hindu.

The two news reports framed the order differently. PTI described it as a relaxation of passport and visa rules for several groups of foreigners. The Hindu's report focused on the new requirement for a visa. Both reflect parts of the text: the exemption from prosecution stays, but continued stay now depends on getting a visa. The ministry has not published an explanatory note, and the order does not say which visa category applies or what happens to people who do not apply.

## Other changes

The order also changes the rules for travel across India's open borders with Nepal and Bhutan. Indian citizens entering or leaving India from those countries by land or air must produce one of the identity documents listed in the government's Visa Manual, which the order now formally defines. Indians using the Nepal or Bhutan borders to travel on to third countries must carry a valid passport and cross only at designated immigration posts.

Nepali and Bhutanese citizens travelling to or from any country other than India, Nepal or Bhutan need valid passports. Those who start their journey in, or pass through, China, Macau, Hong Kong or Pakistan need both a passport and a visa.

Exemptions for registered Sri Lankan Tamil refugees who arrived by 9 January 2015, and for Tibetans who entered on permits issued by the Indian Embassy in Kathmandu, continue; Tibetans must still register and hold a certificate of registration. Indian service personnel travelling on duty with their families on government transport, and the crews of foreign warships coming to India for repairs, are also exempted.

## Background

The 2026 order amends the Immigration and Foreigners (Exemption) Order, 2025, which the Home Ministry notified on 1 September 2025 under the new Act. That order exempted members of the six communities who entered by 31 December 2024 from the passport and visa requirements, The Daily Star reported at the time. Business Today noted that the date went a full decade beyond the cut-off in the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 (CAA).

That gap matters. The CAA offers fast-track citizenship only to members of the six communities who entered India on or before 31 December 2014. People who came after that date cannot apply under it. For them, the 2025 exemption was a protection against prosecution as illegal migrants, not a path to citizenship. The new visa condition means they will now have to take a further step to regularise their stay.

## The Bengal angle

West Bengal has the largest number of people likely to be affected, because most of those who crossed from Bangladesh over the decades settled in the state's border districts. Many belong to the Matua community, a Scheduled Caste Hindu group that originally came from what is now Bangladesh.

The order comes days after Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari promised to speed up CAA hearings. Speaking at a Matua convention in Thakurnagar on 1 November, he said the state would aim to complete hearings for about 2.5 lakh applicants and grant them citizenship by 31 December, The Hindu reported. He also announced Rs 50 crore for Matua development this financial year. Those applicants all entered before the 2014 cut-off. The new visa requirement is aimed at a different group: people who arrived between 2015 and the end of 2024.

## What is not yet clear

- Which visa category the six communities should apply for, and whether there is a fee or deadline.
- What documents people who arrived without papers will need, and whether proof of persecution will be required.
- What happens to people who do not apply, or whose applications are refused.
- Whether the change affects people who have already applied for citizenship under the CAA but are still waiting.

## What happens next

The Home Ministry is expected to set out the procedure in its Visa Manual or in separate instructions. By the time of publication, The Declaration had found no public response to the amendment from the West Bengal government or from political parties in the state. A revision of electoral rolls is due in January, and Adhikari has said CAA applicants will be helped to enrol.
